newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM HOPES 60 COUNTRIES WILL BAN LAND MINES.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM HOPES 60 COUNTRIES WILL BAN LAND MINES.

text.p: Belgium said on Monday it hoped at least 60 countries would sign a treaty to ban land mines before the end of the year.

"I think more than 45 countries will sign the treaty," Belgian Foreign Minister Erik Derycke told a news conference ahead of the four-day Conference on a Global Ban on Anti-personnel Mines which starts on Tuesday.
"I hope for 60, that would be wonderful, but we must be realistic".
Officials from 130 countries are attending the conference to state whether or not they are ready to sign the treaty.
The Brussels conference is a continuation of talks started last year in Ottawa, Canada, which aim to end with the signing of a first anti-mine treaty in December in Ottawa.
"Here in Brussels we will count the heads and see who is with us," Derycke said.
In March 1995 Belgium became the first country to unilaterally renounce the use of mines.
Mines kill an estimated 26,000 people per year -- most of them civilians.

"First we want to get the treaty signed, then we want to globalise it," said Ralph Lysyshyn, Canadian Director-General for International Security. "Then the demining efforts must be stepped up. Those are big challenges ahead of us,"
But regardless of the symbolic success of the Ottawa treaty, not much will change in the field, as China and Russia (the main users and producers of mines) are ignoring the conference.

The U.S. refuses to sign an anti-mine treaty as long as Russia and China do not surrender their mines as well. It has sent observers to the Brussels talks, but prefers to focus its anti-mine effort on the United Nations-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva.
"I hope that countries will realise that the Geneva conference is going nowhere and join the Ottawa process," said Jody Williams, coordinator of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL).
ICBL was set up in 1991-92 by a handful of non-governmental organisations and now represents more than 1,000 NGOs from 60 countries.
The Geneva conference is not expected to produce an anti-mine treaty in the years ahead because its consensus approach allows any participating country to block progress.
"Only a process which is not limited by a consensus approach can get us a treaty in a reasonalbe time," said Canada's Lysyshyn. But he played down the rivalry between the two diplomatic efforts.
"We do see the value of the Geneva talks, they will help to bring round those countries unwilling to sign a treaty now, the Ottawa and Geneva talks complement each other," he said.
The Ottawa treaty will impose a total ban on production, transfer, use and stockpiling of mines.
